# In Fintech, Trust Is the Product and the Channel Is Whoever Already Has It.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/fintech-gtm-trust-distribution/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-14 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A fintech product can offer a better price and a cleaner experience than an established competitor and still struggle to acquire customers, because people are being asked to trust an unfamiliar company with their money, identity or financial information. Paid channels add their own gate: Google now requires financial services advertisers to prove regulatory authorisation in a growing list of countries, with the US and Canada due in early 2027. The channels that work best are the people and platforms customers already trust, given approved facts to repeat and measured on funded, retained use rather than traffic.

*This is strategic guidance from go-to-market work, not legal or regulatory advice.*

## Key points

- Distribution for financial products is partly a trust problem: the customer needs to know who holds the money, what it costs and who answers when it fails.
- Google requires financial ads to show fees and the business address without a click, and verifies financial advertisers by country; it has announced the US and Canada for early 2027.
- The UK FCA says firms remain responsible for every promotion they make or cause to be made, including through influencers and affiliates.
- Trust in close contacts is rising: Edelman's 2026 survey found net trust in neighbours, family and friends up 11 points over recent years.
- A channel producing fewer, better-qualified customers can be worth more than one producing the most traffic. Judge it on funded and retained accounts.

## Trust comes before traffic

People are asked to hand an unfamiliar company their savings, their payroll or their identity documents. A good website alone does not settle that concern. So the distribution question for a fintech is not only where to buy attention. It is how to help the right customer understand what the product does, who is responsible for it and why its claims should be believed.

Paid channels make the point formally. Google's financial products and services policy requires that disclosures be "clearly and immediately visible without needing to click or hover over anything", and that financial ads provide the business's physical address, all associated fees and links to any accreditation they claim. Some locations add a verification step covering licences and registration numbers. Google's financial services verification page lists 42 countries in its location menu, and in Australia, for example, advertisers must prove they are licensed by ASIC before ads run.

The gate is widening. Google launched verification in the UK in September 2021 and reported "a pronounced decline in reports of ads promoting financial scams" afterwards. In October 2026 it announced that the programme will reach the US and Canada in early 2027, working with the American Bankers Association to verify authorised banks. A fintech that relies on paid search should treat proof of authorisation as a launch dependency, not a later task.

An advertising approval is only one obstacle. A prospective customer still asks who holds the money, what happens if something fails, which fees apply and whether a person can be reached. Marketing that promises safety without explaining the protections, or highlights a return while hiding the conditions, may win attention but erodes the trust the business needs. Our piece [Trust is the product](https://lowob.com/research/trust-is-the-product/) sets out the order in which buyers run those checks.

## Work through people and platforms customers already use

The shortest route to trust is through someone the customer already trusts. The Edelman Trust Barometer 2026, a survey of nearly 34,000 people in 28 countries, found that net trust in "my neighbours, family and friends" and "my coworkers" each rose 11 points over recent years, while trust in national government leaders fell 16. Seven in ten respondents said they were unwilling or hesitant to trust someone with different values. Trust is concentrating in people and institutions close to the customer.

There is evidence that customers who arrive through a trusted route are worth more. A study of about 10,000 customers at a German bank by Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte found referred customers had a roughly 18% lower hazard of leaving than comparable customers acquired otherwise, and were at least 16% more valuable over six years.

| Route | Who it is | What it needs from you | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Product and distribution partners | Payroll, accounting, wallet or marketplace platforms whose users fit | Integration work, support ownership, a reason to believe the product suits their users | Slow negotiation; the partner's users may not fit |
| Practitioners and educators | Accountants, advisers, specialist educators and creators | Accurate explanations, approved claims, clear disclosure of any payment | Paid relationships that are not disclosed; unapproved promotions |
| Owned resources | Product guide, pricing page, help centre, customer emails | Plain answers kept current | They are only believed once something else has earned trust |

**Product and distribution partners.** A payroll or accounting platform might introduce a financial service to customers who already rely on its software. A wallet or marketplace can do the same. The partner still has to believe the product is suitable for its users, and its reputation is now attached to yours. Our [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to set the partner's role and pay before recruiting.

**Practitioners and educators.** Accountants, advisers and specialists can explain a product's purpose and limits. A walkthrough or a carefully written comparison answers questions a short ad cannot. Any paid relationship and the relevant disclosures should be clear.

**Owned resources.** A plain product guide, pricing page, help centre and customer emails answer questions after the first encounter. These channels are under the company's control, though customers still need a reason to trust what they say.

None of these routes is guaranteed to be cheap or simple. Partner distribution takes negotiation and integration work, and a creator's audience may be poorly matched. The right channel is the one that reaches suitable customers and produces meaningful product use. [Distribute through whoever already holds the customer](https://lowob.com/research/distribute-through-whoever-already-holds-the-customer/) covers the channel economics.

## Make the proof visible before asking for commitment

Consider a **hypothetical small-business payments platform**. A promising introduction comes from an accounting software company. Before referring its customers, the partner wants to understand reconciliation, failed payments, support ownership and fees. Its customers care less about the technology than about whether payments arrive on time and errors are put right.

The useful marketing response is a clear guide to how payments work, realistic examples of the settlement process, approved descriptions of risk and accessible support details. Those assets help the partner decide whether to refer and help the customer decide whether to sign up.

> When the customer needs trust before acting, distribution should help establish that trust, not just buy more impressions.

Use the same approved facts in outreach, presentations and product pages. When the operating details change, update the material promptly. A partner that finds your deck contradicting your fee page will stop referring before it tells you why.

## Make compliant marketing easier to repeat

Do not treat legal and compliance review as the last obstacle before publishing. Work with the appropriate advisers to build an approved set of claims, disclosures and examples that the team and its partners can use.

The rules reach partners as well as the firm. The FCA's FG24/1 guidance on financial promotions on social media says firms working with affiliate marketers such as influencers "should take proactive responsibility", and that firms "remain responsible for the compliance of every promotion they make or cause to be made." It expects each promotion to be standalone compliant, judged on its own rather than as part of a wider journey, and notes that a breach of section 21 of FSMA is a criminal offence punishable by up to two years' imprisonment. In the US, the FTC tells advertisers they "need to have reasonable programs in place to train and monitor members of their network", and that delegating to an outside company does not relieve them of responsibility.

An approved set may record which products can be advertised in each market, what evidence supports each claim, how fees must be described and what disclosures a creator or affiliate needs. The requirements depend on the product and jurisdiction, and an internal template is not a substitute for legal review. The benefit is practical: sales, partnerships and marketing can move faster without improvising on sensitive claims.

## Judge channels by customers, not just leads

Start with a small number of suitable channels and decide how each will be measured before it launches. A newsletter might produce visits, a partner may introduce qualified businesses and a creator may generate sign-ups. Those actions sit at different distances from revenue.

| Channel output | What it proves | Distance from revenue | Measure that matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Visits | Someone looked | Far | Share who start an application |
| Sign-ups | Someone started | Middle | Share who pass verification and fund |
| Qualified referrals | A trusted party vouched | Middle | Share who complete onboarding |
| First funded transaction | The customer acted | Near | Time from verification to funding |
| Retained use at 90 and 365 days | The trust held | Revenue | Revenue per active funded account, by channel |

For an account-based product, follow the path from qualified referral to completed onboarding, first meaningful financial action and retained use. Include referral fees, incentives and integration work in the cost. A channel producing fewer but better-qualified customers may be worth more than one producing the most traffic. [From funded account to lifetime value](https://lowob.com/research/from-funded-account-to-lifetime-value/) sets out the full chain, and [Referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers paying partners only for what they actually produce.

## lowob takeaways

- **Lead with what customers need to verify.** Explain custody, fees, risk and support clearly, before asking for registration or funds.
- **Treat ad verification as a launch dependency.** Google already verifies financial advertisers by country and plans the US and Canada for early 2027.
- **Choose trusted channels deliberately.** Partners and practitioners help when their audience and the product actually fit.
- **Make claims review reusable.** Approved language and clear disclosures make partnerships easier to operate, and the firm stays responsible for what partners say.
- **Measure meaningful use.** Track qualified onboarding and retention, not just visits or sign-ups.

## Common questions

### How do fintech startups acquire customers when ad platforms restrict financial ads?

By working through people and platforms customers already trust, such as payroll and accounting software, practitioners and educators, and by making sure paid ads meet verification and disclosure rules before launch. Measure each channel on funded, retained accounts.

### Does Google require verification for financial services ads?

In many countries, yes. Google's financial services verification asks advertisers to prove they are authorised by the relevant regulator, and Google announced in October 2026 that the programme will reach the US and Canada in early 2027.

### Is a fintech responsible for what influencers and affiliates say about it?

In the UK, the FCA says firms remain responsible for every promotion they make or cause to be made and should monitor affiliates. In the US, the FTC expects advertisers to train and monitor their endorsers.

### What is the best distribution channel for a fintech?

Usually the one whose audience already trusts the source and fits the product, often a platform or practitioner already serving your customer. Judge it on funded accounts and retention rather than traffic.
